title: The Hajj verses
hook: the pilgrimage, the months, no quarreling, remember Allah at Arafat (2:196–203)

segments.voice: Yesterday: batil, and your line, clean hands. Today, al-Baqarah sets out on a journey.

A stadium letting out. A train station at rush hour. An airport the day before a holiday. Crowds like that test anyone's patience, and the Hajj is a crowd on another scale: pilgrims from far-off countries, in the heat, old and young, all trying to reach the same few places on the same days. Tempers can fray anywhere. In the middle of its laws for this journey, al-Baqarah sets a rule about tempers. Today: the Hajj verses.
screen: `A STADIUM LETTING OUT.` → `A CROWD ON ANOTHER SCALE, IN THE HEAT.` → `A RULE ABOUT TEMPERS.`

segments.voice: Verses one hundred ninety-six to two hundred three are a short handbook for the pilgrimage. Complete the Hajj and the 'umrah for God. The pilgrimage is in the well-known months. Then verse one hundred ninety-seven: whoever takes on the Hajj in them, let there be no indecent talk, no wrongdoing, and no quarreling on the Hajj. The word for quarreling is jidal: arguing, disputing, wrestling with words. It's named where arguments come easily: over a spot in the tent, a push in the crowd, who was first in line. A hadith in Bukhari says whoever performs the Hajj without indecency or wrongdoing returns as on the day their mother bore them. Then the verse turns practical: take provisions for the journey, and the best provision is taqwa, the mindfulness you met on the first page of al-Baqarah. The next verse adds: there is no sin in seeking the bounty of your Lord, which the commentators say means trading during the pilgrimage season. Ordinary life isn't banned. Quarreling is. Then the heart of it: when you press on from Arafat, remember God at the sacred landmark. Arafat is a plain outside Mecca where pilgrims spend one day standing in prayer. A hadith in at-Tirmidhi says simply: the Hajj is Arafah. The day at the center of the journey is spent remembering, not winning arguments.
screen: `A SHORT HANDBOOK FOR THE PILGRIMAGE` · `NO INDECENCY, NO WRONG, NO QUARREL` · `THE BEST PROVISION IS TAQWA` · `THE HAJJ IS ARAFAH`

segments.voice: Picture where today's arguments are likely to start, a family member, a colleague, a comment thread, traffic, and the moment one begins. Then picture letting the other person have the last word, not because they're right, but because you're on a journey and this isn't what you're carrying.
Jidal. Quarreling, disputing, wrestling with words — the one thing al-Baqarah forbids on the Hajj, in a crowd where tempers fray easily. Today's word.
Your line: no quarrel on the journey. The best provision is taqwa. Day three hundred fifty-four, done.

howItsDone: Muslims who are able perform the Hajj once in a lifetime in the month of Dhul-Hijjah; pilgrims enter a state of ihram, avoid quarreling and indecent speech, and spend the Day of Arafah standing in prayer on the plain of Arafat.

chat.says: Why would a pilgrimage need a rule against arguing?
options: Tempers fray in crowds and heat, and 2:197 names no quarreling on the Hajj.
Because pilgrims are banned from talking at all until the journey ends.
It doesn't; the verses only forbid trading during the season.
chat.meaning: Verse 197: let there be no indecent talk, no wrongdoing, and no quarreling on the Hajj, named in a crowd where arguments come easily.

Arafat.meaning: a plain outside Mecca where pilgrims stand in prayer

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 1521 (returns as on the day his mother bore him)

notes: Hadith numbers (Bukhari 1521; Tirmidhi 889) cited from memory; please confirm.
'Around two million people' reflects recent Hajj seasons (numbers vary by year, with restrictions in some years); confirm or soften.
Arafat 'from noon to sunset' describes the usual standing (wuquf); the legal minimum and timing differ by school.
Index hook says 'quarrelling'; the script uses American 'quarreling'.
